title: Polynomial smoothed complexity of FLIP for Max-Cut
formal: Are there absolute constants \(C,a,b>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every simple undirected graph G on n vertices, every \(\varphi \ge 1/2\) and every collection of independent edge-weight distributions supported on \([- 1,1]\) with probability densities bounded by \(\varphi\), the expected length of the longest strictly improving single-vertex-flip path is at most \(C(n+1)^{a}(1+\varphi )^{b}\)?
why: A flagship unresolved explanation of why a canonical PLS local-search algorithm works efficiently on perturbed inputs.
status_note: The ESA 2024 source explicitly retains the arbitrary-graph problem. Searches for subsequent work through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of this expected longest-path target. The general high-probability upper bound and the smoothed 3-FLIP lower bound were separated from the required guarantee. Proofs have not been independently audited.
review_note: Fixed the source’s signed [-1,1] bounded-density model and one-shot independent sampling. Made expectation of the longest path, arbitrary initial cuts, strict improvement and iteration cost explicit. Preserved the expected-time target; did not replace it by a tail bound or a choice of pivot rule.

progress.text: Theorem 1.1 gives the general upper bound \(\varphi n^{O(\sqrt{\log  n})}\) with high probability, controlling every directed path in the improvement graph.

The sparse-graph theorem gives polynomial expected and high-probability bounds for arboricity \(O(\log ^{1- \delta}n)\), with any fixed \(\delta \in\)(0,1]. The paper retains arbitrary graphs as an open case.
The author manuscript gives a smoothed superpolynomial lower bound for 3-FLIP and unperturbed exponential single-FLIP examples; both have a different scope from this target.

sentences: Does FLIP for Max-Cut have polynomial expected path length on every graph under independent bounded-density edge weights?
Each step moves just one vertex and must strictly increase the cut weight.
The expectation controls the longest path after the weights are sampled, including all starting cuts and improving choices.
Polynomial bounds for sparse graph families and a general high-probability bound do not finish this target.
The known smoothed superpolynomial example permits three-vertex moves, while its single-vertex analogue is unperturbed.

upgraded_from.title: Polynomial smoothed complexity of FLIP for Max-Cut

definitions: The graph and one Lebesgue-measurable density \(f_{e}\) for each edge are chosen adversarially before the random weights. Each \(f_{e}\) is nonnegative, integrates to 1 on \([- 1,1]\), and is at most \(\varphi\) almost everywhere; weights \(w_{e}\) are sampled independently once from these densities and then held fixed. They may be negative and need not be identically distributed. A cut is a subset \(S\subseteq V\), with value \(\mathrm{W}_{w}(S)=\Sigma\)_{\(uv\in E\): exactly one of u,v lies in S} \(w_{uv}\). A legal step replaces S by \(S\triangle \{v\}\) for one vertex v, and requires a strictly larger cut value. Define \(\mathrm{L}(G,w)\) as the largest number of steps in any such path, maximized over all starting cuts and all choices of improving vertices after w is known; set \(\mathrm{L}=0\) if there is no step. There are finitely many cuts and strict improvement prevents revisiting one, so \(\mathrm{L}\le 2^{n}- 1\) and its expectation is well-defined. The expectation is over w alone, with the maximum over paths inside it. The resource counted is improving steps, not the bit cost of exact real arithmetic or of sampling distributions. The target concerns all graphs and all allowed densities with one common polynomial. A run ends at a single-flip local maximum, which need not maximize cut value globally.
answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound on \(E_{w}[\mathrm{L}(G,w)]\), or prove its logical negation by exhibiting admissible families that exceed every such polynomial. A bound for selected graph classes or for one favorable pivot rule does not establish the proposition. A rare long path or an unperturbed worst-case instance alone does not refute an expected bound under these density constraints.

context_blocks.title: What FLIP improves
context_blocks.text: The procedure repeatedly moves a vertex to the opposite side when this increases the weight crossing the cut. Different choices can produce different paths, so the question controls the longest one. This includes starting cuts and choices made after seeing the sampled weights, rather than relying on a particular implementation to avoid a bad path.

context_blocks.title: Local optimality has a different goal
context_blocks.text: Consider a four-cycle 1–2–3–4–1 with weights 0.9 on edges 12 and 34 and weights 1 on edges 23 and 41. The cut \(\{1,2\}\) has weight 2, and moving any single vertex decreases it by 0.1. Nevertheless, the alternating cut \(\{1,3\}\) has weight 3.8. Fast termination here would mean finding a state with no improving single move, without asserting that FLIP finds a global maximum.

context_blocks.title: What the smoothing parameter permits
context_blocks.text: The adversary chooses the graph and the distributions, while independent draws supply the randomness. Density bounded by \(\varphi\) prevents a distribution from putting too much probability in an arbitrarily short interval: an interval of length h has probability at most \(\varphi h\). Larger \(\varphi\) permits more concentrated weights, and the requested running-time bound may grow polynomially with \(\varphi\).

context_blocks.title: Known bounds cover only part of the target
context_blocks.text: The general-graph theorem of Chen and coauthors gives \(\varphi n^{O(\sqrt{\log  n})}\) steps with high probability, uniformly over improving paths. Schwartzman proves polynomial expected length when arboricity is \(O(\log ^{1- \delta}n)\) for fixed \(\delta >0\); arboricity is the minimum number of forests needed to partition the edges. This includes sparse graph classes but not arbitrary graphs. The expectation requirement matters: a high-probability statement by itself does not bound the contribution of a long tail.

context_blocks.title: A nearby negative result uses larger moves
context_blocks.text: Michel and Scott show superpolynomial smoothed behavior for 3-FLIP, where a step may move up to three vertices together. Their single-FLIP exponential examples instead concern the setting without random perturbations. Neither statement refutes polynomial expected length for the single-vertex, independently perturbed model here.

Distinguished high-probability bounds, sparse-graph expectation bounds, 3-FLIP lower bounds and unperturbed single-FLIP examples.
